A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same scaling-law study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's additional Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training and evaluation results, including ID/OOD scaling curves, architecture comparisons, and supplementary experiments in Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains original scaling experiments and reports additional baseline comparisons, a distribution-head ablation, dataset diagnostics, and forecast examples.

M1.justification: The patched encoder-only and decoder-only architectures, RoPE, four-component Student-t heads, and forecasting procedures remain unchanged. NLL training was already specified in v1's appendix. The Gaussian-mixture head is an added experimental comparator, not a replacement for the retained model.

E1.justification: Table 3's reported OOD evaluation inventory drops Traffic Weekly and Australian Electricity Demand, although Australian electricity remains in the case studies. Both versions already evaluate LSF and Monash and retain the same pre-training dataset sources; mentioning Monash in v2's main text does not introduce new coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds exponential smoothing (ETS) to Figure 2 and evaluates a Gaussian-mixture-head variant against the Student-t head in Figure 9. The encoder-only, decoder-only, Moirai, and Chronos comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The reported corpus size changes from 14.46B to 16.8B time points, with substantial count revisions in Table 2. Section 3.1 changes the parameter-sweep range from 3K–300M to 1K–100M, and Section 2.3 adds a 0.05 sampling-probability cap. Appendix D replaces MAE with MASE and extends metric evaluation on Monash. These are substantive reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish whether experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing emergence, sample-efficiency, and distribution/metric analyses, v2 adds a Gaussian-versus-Student-t ablation, encoder/decoder training-convergence comparisons, and dataset-characteristic diagnostics (Figures 9–10 and Table 4). Figures 11–13 add actual forecast traces across model sizes, substantially strengthening the evidence examined in the emergence case studies.

E5.justification: v2 introduces shaded bands around parameter-scaling fits in Figures 15–19 and predictive bands labeled 0.5 and 0.9 in Figures 11–13. These add uncertainty displays absent from v1. Their construction is not explained, and neither version supplies repeated-run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: Figure 5 revises numerical fits: encoder/decoder ID data-scaling exponents change from 0.095/0.090 to 0.088/0.087. Newly reported results include ETS MAPE values of 1.81 ID and 0.35 OOD, distribution-head comparisons, dataset diagnostics, and additional Monash and MASE curves; MAE curves disappear. These are revised or additional results, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 4 adds the heuristic relation D proportional to N^(alpha_N/alpha_D), approximated as N^0.8, and derives roughly 1.7 times more data for doubling model size. The original power-law equations and Appendix B derivations remain. The added NTK and learning-dynamics discussions do not provide new proofs.

C1.justification: v1 broadly claims superior encoder-only scalability; v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion restrict the advantage mainly to ID performance and describe similar OOD scalability. The conclusion also changes from emphasizing larger datasets for OOD forecasting to prioritizing model size over data for both ID and OOD. These revise central scientific takeaways.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds quantitative resource-allocation prescriptions and recommends increasing model size rather than extending training. Appendix D adds an NTK-based interpretation of sample efficiency. New Appendix E substantially expands applicability boundaries and unresolved issues concerning multivariate data scarcity, variable correlations, data-mixing bias, architecture choices, and the empirical status of the scaling laws.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the maximum learning rate of 0.001, explicitly states that comparison models share the training setup, and adds a reproducibility statement with a source-code repository link. Conversely, it removes both architecture pseudocode listings from Appendix B. The repository's contents are not verified by the supplied PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds references connecting the discussion to NTK, learning dynamics, data-mixing laws, alternative architectures, and dataset diagnostics, including Jacot, Bordelon, Hashimoto, Ye, and Qiu. The main related-work discussion and positioning around OOD scaling and architecture effects remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes terminology toward NLL, revises architecture-comparison and design-guidance prose, and adds Appendix E plus funding, ethics, and reproducibility statements. The main section sequence and much of the existing exposition remain unchanged, making this targeted revision rather than wholesale restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds diagnostic bar charts, training-convergence plots, multi-panel forecast examples, and Table 4. Appendix metric figures expand to three-distribution comparisons with shaded bands; Figure 2 gains ETS reference lines. Figures and tables are also relocated or resized, with revised axes, legends, and captions.

improvement.justification: The ETS comparison and distribution-head ablation provide useful empirical checks, while narrowing the encoder-superiority claim improves calibration. Forecast examples, dataset diagnostics, and code-access information make the study easier to assess. The gain is limited by removed pseudocode, unexplained uncertainty bands, and the new N^0.8 resource guideline, which is not clearly reconciled with the displayed exponent ratios.
